rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded central cluster and the final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room to slow the gradient afterward if needed.

Test the low-temperature endpoint at the same gradient to distinguish temperature-sensitive overlaps from persistent critical pairs. The current short elution times provide ample margin for the increased retention.

The low-temperature method is strongest, with only two unresolved pairs. A shallower gradient should test whether these pairs can reach baseline resolution while keeping the final peak near the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining critical pair, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. This targets full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Increase gradient duration by one grid step to lift the sole critical pair from R = 1.40 toward full credit. The last peak is expected to remain just under 10 minutes, targeting the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The maximum CRF is already secured; now test a shorter fully resolved separation. Raising the starting organic fraction while slightly shortening the gradient preserves a similar slope and should move the elution window earlier.

Lengthen the previous gradient by one step to recover resolution of the sole critical pair. This may preserve full credit while eluting the last peak earlier than the established maximum-score method.

Test whether a small temperature increase can recover the critical-pair resolution in the faster 20-minute gradient. This probes a route to a shorter maximum-score separation while retaining injection 8 as the fully resolved fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to balance the two central critical pairs at 30 C. The higher start should offset the longer gradient and may deliver full resolution earlier than injection 8.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the remaining R = 1.30 pair, while monitoring the final pair, currently at R = 1.65. This small adjustment targets full resolution with the last peak near eight minutes.

Return to 25 C to restore the final-pair separation, using a shallower gradient to improve the central critical pair. The higher starting organic fraction should keep this candidate faster than the original fully resolved method.
Shorten injection 12 by one gradient step to use its resolution margin and reduce the last-peak time. The critical pair at R = 1.87 may remain fully resolved at this slightly steeper slope.

Shorten the gradient another step to locate the resolution boundary at this starting composition. If the critical pair falls below 1.5, the 28-minute gradient remains the fully resolved fallback for this branch.

With maximum-score methods secured, test a different temperature-selectivity region for a faster fully resolved separation. The shallower gradient than the initial temperature screen may separate overlaps seen at higher temperatures.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a much shallower gradient at the most successful temperature. This may improve central-pair selectivity while shifting the fully resolved elution window earlier.

Test the steeper-gradient side of the central-pair selectivity crossover rather than continuing to flatten the gradient. A reversed elution order could restore separation at substantially shorter retention times, though the late pair may become limiting.

Raise the starting organic fraction to test whether the central pair separates further on the fast-gradient branch. The reduced slope may also help preserve the late pair, which was just fully resolved in injection 17.

Increase the starting organic fraction one more step, following the improved central-pair resolution from injections 17 to 18. This targets full resolution with a last-peak time below five minutes while monitoring the neighboring pairs.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved gradient by one step to test its resolution margin. Injection 19 remains the fallback if either the central or late critical pair drops below 1.5.

Restore the fully resolving gradient duration and raise temperature one step to seek a shorter elution window through altered selectivity. Monitor the central cluster closely, retaining injection 19 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to recover the central-pair separation lost with faster slopes. This explores whether the elution window can move earlier while preserving full resolution at 25 C.

Narrow the gradient window while preserving injection 19's successful slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute. All eight peaks should elute before this shorter gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed method.

Test a slope halfway between the fully resolved injection 19 and the faster but under-resolved injection 20. This locates the speed boundary more closely; the confirmed maximum-score method remains available if the central pair falls below 1.5.

Back off to the confirmed fully resolving slope of 0.05 per minute and shorten the programmed gradient to four minutes. Its outlet endpoint at 4.65 minutes remains after the observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should preserve CRF 1.000.
